bronte_walker.text: {greeting} Top Withens is just there. Emily walked these moors in every weather. You can see why she wrote about wild, windy places.

then.text: Off back to the Parsonage? Tell the curator the wind was in fine voice.
You saw off our Heathcliff? Good. He's been howling at me since Tuesday. Stand here a minute. Listen. That roar in the wind is what 'wuthering' means.
Now you've stood where Emily stood. Tell the curator you've done Withens.

else.text: Doing the Parsonage trail? You'll want to get past the brooding lad by the ruin first. He won't let anyone enjoy the view in peace.
There are signposts up here in Japanese as well as English. Visitors come from all over the world for the Brontës.

bronte_keeper_tale.text: {greeting} This one's called Keeper, after Emily's dog. He's a terrier, mind, not a mastiff. He has the attitude of a mastiff.
Emily once punished the real Keeper for lying on the beds, and he went for her. She beat him with her bare fists. They were best friends after. Different times.

haworth_setts.text: {greeting} Steepest Main Street in Yorkshire, I reckon. The setts are lovely on a dry day. On a wet day, hold on to summat.
There's a Victorian weekend every winter where everyone dresses up. Our postman did it in a top hat. He's kept the top hat.

haworth_steam.text: {greeting} Everyone on this railway is a volunteer, from the porters to the drivers. We do it for love. And the smell of coal smoke.
Oakworth station's down the line. They filmed The Railway Children there. People still turn up waving red petticoats.

haworth_ghost.text: They say Haworth's one of the most haunted villages in England. Grey ladies, headless horsemen, a monk on the church steps.
Most nights I see nothing. Some nights the fog comes down Main Street and I see quite a lot of nothing very clearly.

haworth_victorian.text: {greeting} Do you like my bonnet? I made it. It's historically accurate apart from the fleece lining. The Brontës would have killed for fleece.
